articles.title: Quantity and counting
body: A collection has zero members if it is empty. To count a finite collection, choose its members and pair each with exactly one number in a counting sequence beginning at one. The last number used tells how many members there are. Counting the same members in a different order gives the same result.

Two collections have equal quantity when each member of one can be paired with a unique member of the other and all members are paired. A group of three stones and a group of three marks have equal counts even though their members differ.
articles.limitations: The quantity depends on what was selected as a member. Grouping pairs of stones as single items changes the question being counted. Numeral forms and reading directions are conventions.
articles.status: Source-checked draft — independent human review pending

articles.title: Arithmetic and relationships
body: Addition can describe joining collections with no shared members. Joining a pair of marks and three more marks gives five: 2 + 3 = 5. Equality says that both sides represent the same value. Removing a group of three from the five leaves two: 5 − 3 = 2.

Multiplication can count equally sized groups: three groups of four objects contain twelve objects. Dividing twelve into groups of four gives three groups. Dividing five whole objects into two equally sized groups leaves one object over if the objects are kept whole.
articles.limitations: These examples use whole objects. Fractions and negative numbers extend the operations to other cases. Division by zero has no defined value in ordinary arithmetic.

articles.title: Geometry and measurement
body: Geometry describes positions, shapes and their relationships. When two straight directions meet, an angle describes their separation. Comparing two lengths by division gives a ratio. An object that is twice as long as another has the same length ratio whether the lengths are measured in small or large units.

To label positions on a flat surface, choose an origin and two perpendicular axes. In a common convention, two numbers say how far to move along the first and second axes from the origin, using the stated units and directions. Changing the origin changes the numbers used for a point.
articles.limitations: The grid is a flat mathematical model. Human orientation conventions and coordinate labels must be established before using a diagram to give directions.

articles.title: Binary and information
body: Binary notation uses two symbols, written as 0 and 1 in this archive. In common positional binary the places have weights one, two, four, eight and onward from right to left. The sequence 101 therefore represents one group of four, no groups of two, and one more, a total of five.

Two distinguishable states can represent the symbols, as with holes and unmarked positions on a punched card. The record needs a convention for where to start, which direction to read, how to group positions and whether a group encodes a number, a character or a measurement.
articles.limitations: The meaning of a bit sequence depends on the surrounding agreement about its boundaries and mapping. A photographed IBM card has its own historical code, while the Centauri raster uses other rules.

articles.title: Ratios and proportional relationships
body: A ratio compares quantities by division. The ratio 2 to 3 is equal to 4 to 6 because both quantities increased by the same factor. If both quantities are lengths, convert them to the same unit before comparing them. A rate such as distance traveled per time compares different kinds of quantities and carries units.

A proportion states that two ratios are equal. If a drawing uses one length unit to represent five of the same unit on an object, a feature three units long in the drawing represents fifteen units. This calculation relies on the same scale factor being used for every length in the comparison.
articles.limitations: A projection of a large curved surface onto a flat map can vary in scale. The scale of a lens image can also depend on the depth of the object.

articles.title: Powers and orders of magnitude
body: An exponent shows repeated multiplication when it is a positive whole number. In base ten, ten to the third power is 10 × 10 × 10, or one thousand. A negative integer exponent gives a reciprocal. Ten to the power of minus three is one thousandth.

Scientific notation can express a value as a number with magnitude at least one and less than ten multiplied by a power of ten. For example, 3,200 may be written as 3.2 × 10³. Multiplying a quantity by ten changes it by one order of magnitude. Comparing widely different scales becomes easier when both are expressed in the same units.
articles.limitations: Writing a value with a power of ten does not make a measurement more accurate. Units, significant figures and uncertainty describe different aspects of the measurement.

articles.title: Matter and atoms
body: Atoms have a compact nucleus surrounded by electrons. The number of protons in the nucleus defines the element. A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons. Changing the number of electrons changes its electric charge, giving an ion.
Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons. These forms are isotopes. For example, carbon-12 and carbon-13 each have six protons. They have six and seven neutrons, respectively.
articles.limitations: Atomic images depend on how an instrument interacts with a specimen and displays the result. A drawing with fixed electron tracks is also a simplified representation.

articles.title: Energy and physical interactions
body: Energy measures the state and changes of physical systems. A falling object gives an example. In a model with negligible air resistance, the gravitational potential energy of the object–Earth system decreases while the object's kinetic energy increases.

Energy can transfer between systems. An object sliding to a stop on a rough surface warms the object and the surface, as some organized motion becomes internal energy. In an isolated system the total energy is conserved even as the form or location of the energy changes.
articles.limitations: The accounting depends on which objects and interactions are included in the system. The falling-object example uses an everyday mechanical approximation.

articles.title: Molecules and chemical bonds
body: Atoms can form molecules. In a covalent bond, a pair of atoms shares electrons. A water molecule consists of an oxygen atom covalently bonded to two hydrogen atoms. The atoms form a bent arrangement.

Chemical behavior depends on composition and arrangement. For example, carbon dioxide is linear and water is bent. Combined with differences in how different atoms attract shared electrons, geometry affects the distribution of electric charge and how a molecule interacts with its surroundings.
articles.limitations: A ball-and-stick drawing is a geometrical model. The sticks and size of the spheres do not depict the detailed distribution of electrons.

articles.title: Stars, galaxies and the Solar System
body: A star such as the Sun emits energy sustained for much of its life by fusion. The Solar System contains the Sun and the objects bound to it by gravity, including planets, smaller orbiting bodies and their moons. Earth follows an orbit around the Sun.

The Sun is one of the many stars in the Milky Way. A galaxy is a larger gravitational system with stars, gas, dust and other matter. Images of the Solar System and a distant galaxy show different scales and kinds of structure. The Solar System montage assembles separate pictures.
articles.limitations: Astronomical maps and composites may combine different instruments or times. Read the provenance and scale before comparing apparent sizes on the page.

articles.title: Formation of the Solar System
body: The Sun and its planetary system developed from material in a cloud of gas and dust. Gravity drew material together. A rotating disk surrounded the growing star. In the disk, small solid particles grew into larger bodies through accumulation and some collisions.

Meteorites preserve material from the early Solar System. Observations of disks around young stars provide another way to investigate how planetary systems form. Planet formation concerns the assembly of a planetary body. The emergence of living systems is a separate question.
articles.limitations: This is a simplified formation model; the detailed history of individual bodies remains under investigation.

articles.title: Electromagnetic radiation
body: Electromagnetic radiation can carry energy through empty space. A wave description uses wavelength, the distance between equivalent points such as adjacent crests, and frequency, the number of cycles per unit time. In a vacuum, wavelength multiplied by frequency gives the speed of light. Radio waves have longer wavelengths than the radiation human eyes normally detect.

An instrument can measure intensity in a range of wavelengths and assign colors to display those measurements. The result can show structures invisible to unaided eyes. The display colors then belong to the visualization convention and need the instrument's legend to interpret.
articles.limitations: A wave description is sufficient for these examples. Some measurements require describing transfers of energy in discrete quanta.

articles.title: How stars change
body: Stars form when gravity gathers gas within clouds. If the center becomes sufficiently hot and dense, nuclei can fuse there. For much of the Sun's lifetime, fusion converts hydrogen to helium in the core. Energy transported to the surface escapes as radiation.

Mass influences how a star develops. A star like the Sun can expand into a red giant and eventually leave a compact white dwarf. Some much more massive stars undergo core collapse. Some such collapses produce a supernova, and a neutron star or black hole can remain.
articles.limitations: These are illustrative paths for single stars. Rotation, chemical composition and interactions with companion stars can change events and outcomes.

articles.title: Heat, temperature and matter
body: When two objects at different temperatures make thermal contact, energy tends to move from the warmer object to the cooler one. This transfer due to a temperature difference is called heat. A temperature describes the thermal condition of a system. A large and a small volume of the same liquid can share a temperature while containing different amounts of internal energy.

A phase is a form of matter with uniform physical properties. Ice and liquid water are different phases that can coexist during melting. Whether a substance is solid, liquid or gas can depend on both temperature and pressure. Boiling begins when the vapor pressure of the liquid reaches the surrounding pressure.
articles.limitations: These examples describe familiar materials close to thermal equilibrium. Temperature alone cannot determine the phase without additional conditions.
articles.rights: Original project text; publication license pending

articles.title: Gravity and orbits
body: Gravity changes the motion of objects. In Newton's model, two point masses attract each other. For the same masses, doubling the separation reduces the force to one quarter. Outside nearly spherical bodies the model uses distance between their centers.

An orbit can be understood as continuing free fall. A spacecraft moving sideways falls toward Earth while its path curves around the planet. If one body is much more massive, many bound paths are approximated by an ellipse with that mass at one focus. The period is the time for one circuit of a repeating orbit.
articles.limitations: These examples use a Newtonian model with simplified bodies. Gravity from other bodies, drag, propulsion and relativistic effects can matter in more precise calculations.
articles.rights: Original project text; publication license pending

articles.title: What light spectra reveal
body: A spectrometer separates radiation by wavelength and measures how much arrives in different bands. A hot dense object can give a broad spectrum. A dilute excited gas can emit strongly at particular wavelengths, appearing as bright lines in a graph or image.

When broad-spectrum light passes through a cooler gas, some wavelengths can be absorbed more strongly, appearing as dark lines. Comparing observed patterns with laboratory spectra helps identify atoms or molecules along the path. A spectrum of a star therefore gives evidence beyond the color seen by an eye.
articles.limitations: Multiple substances and physical conditions can contribute to the same observation. Motion can shift wavelengths and finite instrument resolution can blend lines. A single line may not identify its source.
articles.rights: Original project text; publication license pending

articles.title: Atoms rearranged in chemical reactions
body: In an ordinary chemical reaction, atoms are rearranged into different combinations. Existing bonds can change or break, and new bonds can form. Reactants are the substances taking part at the start. Products are substances formed by the reaction.

A chemical equation can count the atoms before and after a reaction. Two hydrogen molecules have four hydrogen atoms in total. One oxygen molecule has two oxygen atoms. Together they account for the atoms in two water molecules. A balanced equation conserves the number of atoms of each element.
articles.limitations: The counts in a balanced equation do not specify when a reaction will occur or how fast. The example describes atom accounting without forming a laboratory procedure.

articles.title: Earth as a planet
body: Earth is a rocky planet with surface oceans and an atmosphere. Below the crust and mostly solid mantle lie a liquid outer core and a solid inner core.

As Earth rotates, most locations periodically move through light and shadow. Earth's rotational axis is tilted relative to the perpendicular to its orbital plane. As the planet travels around the Sun, each hemisphere receives different amounts of sunlight at different times of year.
articles.limitations: Geographic coordinates are conventions; the planet itself provides physical reference features.

articles.title: Water and the water cycle
body: Water moves among the ocean, atmosphere, soil, organisms, rivers, lakes and ice. Evaporation transfers water from a liquid surface to water vapor. Cooling can produce droplets or ice in clouds. Precipitation can return water to the surface, where some runs into rivers or seeps into the ground.

Near standard atmospheric pressure of 101,325 pascals, pure water freezes near 273 kelvin and boils near 373 kelvin. Changing pressure changes the temperature at which it boils. Dissolved material can also shift freezing and boiling behavior. These are examples of how the same substance changes form.
articles.limitations: The rounded temperatures describe pure water near equilibrium. A picture of a cloud shows droplets or ice rather than gaseous water vapor.

articles.title: Atmosphere, climate and geology
body: Sunlight delivers energy to Earth. The surface and atmosphere absorb part of it, and the Earth system emits energy to space largely as infrared radiation. Water moving through the atmosphere and ocean can redistribute energy between different regions.

Weather describes atmospheric conditions on short timescales. Climate describes patterns such as typical temperatures and precipitation, and how variable they are over much longer intervals. A storm image records one event. A collection of measured conditions over many years supports judgments about a changing pattern.

Climate and geology interact at the surface. Rain and ice can weather rock and carry sediment. The movement of tectonic plates can build relief and change the surface that winds and water flow across.
articles.limitations: A picture, such as the hurricane image, can document an event without establishing a long-term trend. Different questions about climate require different geographical and time scales.

articles.title: Water reservoirs and transport
body: Water is distributed across Earth's ocean, inland water bodies, ice, atmosphere, soil and underground spaces. A reservoir can retain water for very different durations depending on its location and the mechanisms moving water into and out of it.

Water can enter the atmosphere from surfaces or plants, return as precipitation, infiltrate the ground, or flow through rivers toward other reservoirs. Solar heating and gravity help drive these transfers. A diagram of the cycle describes recurring processes rather than a single path that every molecule follows.
articles.limitations: A global conceptual diagram cannot describe local water availability, contamination or changes through time.

articles.title: Plate tectonics
body: Earth's rigid outer layer, the lithosphere, includes the crust and uppermost mantle. It is broken into plates that move relative to one another. Where plates separate at ocean ridges, hot material can rise and form new crust. At some convergent boundaries one plate descends into the mantle beneath another. At transform boundaries plates move past one another.

Patterns of earthquakes, volcanic activity and magnetic stripes on the ocean floor support this model. Instruments can also measure the motion of locations on Earth's surface over time. Satellites can observe surface forms such as the East African Rift, where parts of the lithosphere are being pulled apart.
articles.limitations: Surface shape alone does not establish the motion or whether a nearby earthquake is imminent. Plate boundaries can be wide or complex.

articles.title: Coupled atmosphere and ocean
body: The ocean and atmosphere exchange energy and matter across their boundary. Winds can drive surface currents. Differences in water temperature and salinity affect density and help drive deeper movements. Currents redistribute heat across an otherwise unevenly heated planet.

When water evaporates, it takes energy from its surroundings. Water vapor carries this energy and can release energy during condensation. Observing wind, surface temperature and humidity together helps investigators estimate exchanges that cannot be read from a single photograph.
articles.limitations: Ocean and atmosphere interactions occur at different time and length scales. Currents and individual cloud patterns can vary with depth, season and location.

articles.title: Soils, weathering and erosion
body: Weathering breaks down or alters material in place. Water can react with minerals, and expanding ice can force open cracks. Erosion moves material by water, wind, ice or gravity. When the transporting flow loses the capacity to carry some particles, those particles may accumulate as sediment.

Soils develop from parent material affected by climate, organisms, relief and time. They can contain minerals, organic material, water and air. Soil layers can differ in composition and structure. Burrowing, roots, decomposition and movement of water help change them over time.
articles.limitations: Landscape photographs illustrate surface forms. Soil composition, formation time and rates of erosion need local measurements or geological evidence.

articles.title: Cells and metabolism
body: Cells are the basic units of cellular organisms. A cell membrane helps regulate exchanges between the cell and its surroundings. The cell uses ribosomes to assemble proteins, and its internal structures let different processes take place in the same small space.

Bacteria and archaea lack a membrane-bound nucleus. In most eukaryotic cells a nucleus encloses much of the genetic material. Some specialized cells, including mature human red blood cells, lose their nucleus. Mitochondria in eukaryotes and chloroplasts in plants and many algae descend from bacteria that became incorporated into ancestral cells.
Metabolism is the set of chemical reactions in which a cell transforms matter and uses or stores energy. Multicellular organisms distribute some of this work among specialized cells and tissues.
articles.limitations: The cell diagram depicts one general form of animal cell. Membranes, surface structures, organelles and dimensions vary widely.

articles.title: DNA and inheritance
body: In cellular life, deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) carries inherited information. Its strands consist of linked units with four common kinds of bases. The bases occur in sequences, and complementary bases can pair so that each strand can guide the copying of the other.

Changes in base sequence are called mutations. Recombination can rearrange existing variation. Inheritance passes some of this information to new cells and to descendants, while genes and environments both influence how organisms develop.
articles.limitations: Genes operate within cells and environments; they do not determine every trait independently.

articles.title: Evolution and biodiversity
body: The frequency of inherited variants can change across generations. One mechanism is natural selection. In a particular environment, individuals with different inherited traits can differ in how many descendants they leave. A variant contributing to greater reproductive success can become more frequent.

Frequency can also change by chance, especially in small populations. That process is genetic drift. Mutation creates new variants, and gene flow moves variants between populations. Shared features and genetic comparisons provide evidence for common ancestry.
articles.limitations: An advantageous trait in one environment can be costly in another. Evolution has no fixed destination. Several mechanisms can operate on the same population at once.

articles.title: Ecosystems and food webs
body: An ecosystem includes organisms and the parts of their surroundings with which they interact. In a food web, a link can trace matter and energy transferred when one organism consumes another. Producers use light or chemical reactions to make organic material. Consumers obtain material and energy by feeding on other organisms or their remains.

Energy enters and leaves local ecosystems. Elements such as carbon and nitrogen can be recycled between living bodies, air, water and sediment. Earth's biosphere comprises the regions where life occurs and includes many connected ecosystems.
articles.limitations: Food webs are variable and interdependent, not simple linear chains.

articles.title: Genes, chromosomes and genomes
body: A genome is the full set of an organism's genetic information. A chromosome is an organized DNA molecule with associated material. A gene is a region of DNA whose information contributes to making a functional RNA or protein.

During protein synthesis, a ribosome reads the sequence in messenger RNA in groups of three bases. These groups specify amino acids or signals, such as when to stop. Other portions of a genome may influence when genes are used or have functions unrelated to making a protein.
Inherited variation can influence how traits develop. The influence can depend on other inherited variants and on conditions during life.
articles.limitations: The organization and interpretation of genomes vary among organisms; the genetic code has some exceptions.

articles.title: Characteristics and origins of known life
body: Earth's cellular organisms maintain boundaries, exchange matter and energy with their surroundings, and carry information that can be inherited. Across generations, populations can evolve. A characteristic shared by living populations need not be expressed by every individual. For example, individual animals that cannot reproduce remain living organisms.

Evidence from ancient rocks and from comparisons among living organisms helps researchers reconstruct some of life's history. How early chemical systems began to maintain themselves, reproduce with variation and evolve remains unsettled. Scientists study several possible pathways; a demonstration that one step can happen leaves the whole historical sequence open.
articles.limitations: The archive describes observed properties of terrestrial life. An agreed universal definition and an independent extraterrestrial example are still missing.

articles.title: RNA and proteins
body: Ribonucleic acid, or RNA, is a family of molecules built from linked units. Messenger RNA can carry a copy of information from DNA to a ribosome. Other RNAs help the ribosome read the message and assemble amino acids in sequence. Some RNAs take part in regulation or catalyze chemical reactions.

An amino acid chain can fold into a shape that enables a protein's function. Proteins can provide mechanical structure, carry molecules or accelerate reactions. Changes in a chain or in its surroundings can change how it folds or functions.
articles.limitations: Gene expression and protein assembly vary across organisms and cellular circumstances. This account introduces shared roles at the level needed to read later biology articles.

articles.title: Photosynthesis and cellular respiration
body: In oxygen-producing photosynthesis, cells use light energy to build organic molecules from carbon dioxide. Water supplies electrons and oxygen is released. Plants, algae and cyanobacteria carry out this process. The chloroplasts visible in the leaf micrograph are sites of photosynthesis in plant cells.

During aerobic cellular respiration, cells transfer energy from organic compounds into forms that can support their work. Oxygen accepts electrons at the end of a series of transfers. Cells of photosynthetic plants also respire. Other metabolic pathways enable living cells to obtain energy when oxygen is unavailable.
articles.limitations: This overview describes familiar pathways. Some forms of photosynthesis do not release oxygen, and the availability and use of light and oxygen vary among environments.

articles.title: Microorganisms, plants, fungi and animals
body: Microorganisms are organisms studied at scales that often require a microscope. They occur in multiple branches of life. Bacteria and archaea each form major groups, while many other microscopic organisms are eukaryotes, with a different internal cell organization.

Among eukaryotes, many plants use light energy to make organic material. Fungi obtain nutrients from material around them, and many decompose remains or associate with other organisms. Animals are multicellular and acquire organic nutrients from other organisms or their products. Ferns, mushrooms and fish illustrate some of these groups.
articles.limitations: Microorganism describes scale and mode of observation. It is a different kind of category from a lineage. The portraits show examples from many distinct branches, and no one photograph defines a group.

articles.title: Biodiversity and extinction
body: Biodiversity includes variation among individuals, among species and among ecosystems. Different species rely on different features of their surroundings. A forest and a coral reef differ in habitat, structure and exchanges of matter and energy, even without counting individual organisms.

A species becomes extinct if its last living members die. A species can also disappear from part of its former range while surviving elsewhere. Human changes to land and oceans, direct exploitation, climate change, pollution and introduced organisms can reduce local or global biodiversity.
articles.limitations: Many species are poorly observed. Estimates of threatened species and of losses depend on observation, definitions, date and the scope of the assessment.

articles.title: Human anatomy and physiology
body: Anatomy describes the structure of bodies. Physiology describes how those structures work. A bone, muscle and tendon can be examined as objects and also studied together to explain how a person moves a joint.

Human tissues contain cells organized for different roles. Tissues form organs such as the heart, and organs cooperate in systems. A structure can serve several systems. For example, the tongue helps move food, bears structures involved in taste, and participates in speech.

articles.title: Human development and inheritance
body: Development includes changes in the structure and function of the body over time. Early in development, repeated cell division produces groups of cells. Cells differentiate as they take on distinct roles, such as contributing to muscle or nervous tissue.

Inherited variants help shape biological development together with conditions before and after birth. During growth and aging, bodies change at different rates. For example, inherited differences and lived conditions can contribute to differences in mobility in later life.

articles.title: Cognition and language
body: Cognition describes processes such as attending to information, remembering, learning and solving problems. Seeing an object uses sensory signals. Recognizing it can also depend on prior experience. Cognitive abilities and experiences vary within a person over time and across people.

A language gives a community shared ways to combine meaningful expressions. Speech uses sounds. Signed languages use movements and spatial relationships of hands, face and body. A writing system uses visible or tactile marks to record parts of language. The sign-language photograph documents a specific exchange and does not define what the signs mean.
articles.limitations: There is no one-to-one mapping across all languages and experiences. The archive's language bridge supplies examples whose interpretations need testing.

articles.title: Organization of the human body
body: The human body can be described at several scales. Molecules form cellular structures; cells cooperate within tissues; tissues form organs; and organs work together in systems. These levels describe relationships within a single living organism.

The heart, blood and blood vessels form a transport system. The respiratory system exchanges gases with the surroundings, while muscles and skeletal structures enable movement. Other systems coordinate responses, process nutrients and maintain internal conditions. Their functions overlap: no organ system is completely independent of the rest of the body.
articles.limitations: The model describes general human biology; individuals differ in anatomy, development and function.

articles.title: Skeleton, joints and muscles
body: Bones support the body, protect some organs and provide surfaces on which muscles can act. A joint is where bones meet. Some joints allow a large range of motion, while others allow very little. Tendons transmit force from muscles to bones. At the elbow, muscle force can bend or straighten the arm.

Skeletal muscle can shorten as its fibers generate tension. Motion usually involves several muscles and coordinated signals from the nervous system. The pottery photograph shows one activity in which the hand's joints, muscles and sense of touch work together.
articles.limitations: An articulated museum skeleton shows the arrangement of bones. It omits living tissue and some features that vary with age, development, disability and individual anatomy.

articles.title: Circulation and breathing
body: The heart pumps blood through two connected circuits. The right side sends blood to the lungs. Blood returning from the lungs enters the left side, which pumps it through vessels to the rest of the body. Small vessels called capillaries exchange materials with surrounding tissues.

Air enters the lungs during inhalation. At small air sacs called alveoli, oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide moves from the blood into air that can be exhaled. The blood transports oxygen to tissues and carries carbon dioxide away. Breathing and cellular respiration describe different processes.
articles.limitations: The diagram shows the flow of blood after birth at a simplified scale. The fetal circulation uses different pathways, and real blood vessels form branching networks.

articles.title: Digestion and nutrient absorption
body: Digestion changes food into forms the body can use. Teeth break food into smaller pieces. In the stomach and intestines, movement mixes the contents with fluids, and enzymes split many large molecules. The liver makes bile, which helps process fats, and the pancreas supplies several digestive enzymes.

Much of the absorption of nutrients takes place across the wall of the small intestine. The large intestine absorbs water, and its microorganisms transform some compounds that reach it. Circulation distributes absorbed materials to tissues.
articles.limitations: Food and meals vary across communities and individuals. These descriptions explain physiology without specifying a diet or treating one daily practice as universal.

articles.title: Nervous system and senses
body: The brain and spinal cord form the central nervous system. Nerves connect it to much of the body. Neurons convey signals through changes in electrical activity and often communicate with other cells using chemical signals. These networks support movement, coordination and the processing of information.

Receptor cells respond to particular kinds of input. Cells in the retina respond to light. Vibrations transmitted through the ear can move sensory cells in the inner ear and produce signals. Other receptors respond to mechanical force, chemicals or temperature. Signals from many receptors are combined during perception.
articles.limitations: The eye photograph shows an external part of the eye. The ear record depicts a model and the microscopy record shows rat neurons. Human sensory experience and abilities vary.

articles.title: Immune function and homeostasis
body: Homeostasis describes regulated conditions in the body, such as temperature, staying within ranges compatible with function. When body temperature rises, evaporation of sweat can remove heat. This is a feedback process because the response changes the condition that helped trigger it.

Several systems help protect tissue from damage and infection. Skin and other barriers restrict entry. Immune cells can respond to signs of damage or foreign material; some mount more targeted responses. Antibodies can bind specific targets, and some immune cells persist after a response, supporting a faster response on later encounters.
articles.limitations: Normal ranges and responses vary across people and circumstances. These examples describe basic physiology, and immune activity can also damage healthy tissue.

articles.title: Reproduction, development and variation
body: In sexual reproduction, fertilization joins an egg and sperm, forming a cell called a zygote. As cells divide, groups specialize into tissues. During development in the uterus, the placenta supports exchanges of materials between the pregnant individual and the developing organism. Ultrasound imaging uses echoes to show some structures before birth.

Human bodies continue to change after birth. Genes, environments and lived conditions influence development and aging. Individual variation includes differences in body proportions, sensory abilities and rates of change. Images of people at different life stages can show examples of variation.
articles.limitations: Life stages are descriptive and can be defined differently by culture and purpose. A single ultrasound and a single group portrait show individuals at particular times.

articles.title: Human history and communities
body: Material remains, oral histories and written records give different kinds of evidence about people in the past. A tool can show manufacturing choices. An oral account can preserve names and relationships. A written account can record transactions, while expressing its author's interests and point of view.

Fossil and genetic evidence place the origin of Homo sapiens in Africa. Agricultural histories vary by region. Archaeologists have evidence for local plant domestication in eastern North America, and clay tablets from ancient Mesopotamia document one early writing tradition. These examples answer different historical questions and belong to different regional timelines.

Spaceflight examples have more precise recorded dates. Sputnik 1 became the first artificial satellite to orbit Earth in 1957. In 1969 the Apollo 11 crew carried out the first human landing on the Moon.
articles.limitations: Surviving evidence is unevenly distributed. New findings can change an interpretation, and a few examples cannot represent all historical experiences.

articles.title: Institutions, exchange and ideas
body: Institutions are durable patterns of rules and practices that structure social activity. Some are formal, with stated rules and roles. Others, such as conventions for asking or granting help, persist through shared expectations. Practices can differ between regions and change within a community.

Exchange is one way people distribute goods, services and labor. Markets are one form, and gifts and shared obligations are others. The photographed market in Onitsha shows one place where people trade. It cannot show the full set of rules or relationships under which they do so.

articles.title: Human origins and migration
body: Fossils preserve parts of past bodies. Comparisons of bone shape and geological dating help place them in time. Fossils from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco show a combination of older and more recent-looking traits. Researchers reported a date of roughly 315,000 years, with a stated uncertainty of 34,000 years, for heated stone artifacts from associated deposits.

Early Homo sapiens lived in Africa. Evidence from fossils, archaeology and ancestry shows people later spread to other continents. Repeated movement, separation and contact shaped human populations. Today's shared ancestry and diversity reflect many of these histories.
articles.limitations: A site dates particular evidence. It does not mark the instant a species began. Population history and the times and paths of some migrations remain under investigation.

articles.title: Agriculture and settlement histories
body: Cultivation and domestication describe different changes. Cultivation means people tend plants or growing conditions. Domestication involves inherited changes in a population through interaction with people across generations. Archaeologists identify some of these changes by comparing preserved plant remains. Eastern North America is one region with evidence for local plant domestication.

Settlements have many forms and may change with seasons, food sources and social ties. At Mesa Verde, in what is now Colorado, Ancestral Pueblo people farmed land on the mesa tops. Changes in the recorded structures show that the landscape held different kinds of settlements over time, including cliff dwellings.
articles.limitations: Cultivating food did not cause every society to follow the same path. Surviving plant remains, archaeological sites and community histories give different parts of the record.

articles.title: Writing and durable records
body: Writing uses recurring marks and conventions to represent language. Some records begin with practical information about quantities or people. The Metropolitan Museum of Art interprets the clay tablet in the image library as a probable account of barley and emmer wheat. Its material helps it survive, and understanding the marks still depends on comparing many records.

Other writing traditions left different materials and purposes. At Yin Xu in China, inscriptions on oracle bones are evidence of writing in the late Shang period. Written documents can preserve evidence of transactions, names or speech. Surviving documents reflect particular authors, institutions and conditions of preservation.

articles.title: Agriculture and engineering
body: Agriculture manages plants, animals, soils and water to produce food and other materials. Practices differ with climate, species, land, knowledge and community needs. Managing water in a crop field changes growing conditions and may also affect nearby waterways.

Engineering designs systems for specified purposes under constraints. A team can state a need, compare possible designs, build and test a model and revise the design in light of results. For example, a device that moves water can be tested for the amount moved per unit time and the energy it requires.
articles.limitations: Engineering choices involve concrete trade-offs. Crop yields, water supply, environmental impact, labor and cost can lead to different decisions about a shared task.

articles.title: Computing and artificial intelligence
body: A digital computer represents instructions and values as discrete states. In a stored-program design, a processor reads instructions from memory and follows them to change or compare stored values. An input acquires data from outside the machine. An output sends a result to a person or another device.

An artificial intelligence system can produce predictions, classifications, recommendations or other outputs for a specified purpose. In one common approach, machine learning uses examples to fit a model that can produce outputs on new data. Performance can change when data and conditions differ from those used to develop the system.

articles.title: Flight and space exploration
body: An aircraft moving through a surrounding gas can generate aerodynamic forces. A wing redirects air and experiences lift. Weight acts toward Earth. Drag opposes motion through the air, and many aircraft use propulsion to supply thrust.

A spacecraft with its own propellant can accelerate by expelling it, even in near-vacuum. Rockets carry launch vehicles beyond dense air. Once in orbit, a spacecraft can continue to fall around a larger body while its instruments observe Earth or distant objects. Some spacecraft carry people and many operate without a crew.

articles.title: Measurement and instruments
body: A measurement assigns a value to a specified quantity using a method and a reference. A marked length standard, for example, permits comparisons at the scale of its intervals. Calibration establishes how readings relate to reference values under stated conditions.

Measurement results have uncertainty. Repeating a measurement can show how readings vary under the repeat conditions. Close agreement among repeated readings does not eliminate a bias. An instrument that gives the same reading each time can still disagree with a reference standard.
articles.limitations: An instrument result needs its quantity definition, method, reference conditions and uncertainty. A photograph of an instrument does not establish a record's calibration.

articles.title: Art, music and daily experience
body: People make visual objects, sounds, movements and stories that can express experiences and carry knowledge. A song can accompany work or a celebration. Cloth can protect a body and reflect skills or meanings learned among its makers. Games can be recreational and also teach shared rules or skills.

Knowledge about making things and organizing daily life can pass between people through language, imitation, demonstration and participation. Habits vary between households and communities. A museum record of a musical instrument and a photograph of weaving document different practices. Each leaves out sound, movement and the wider circumstances of use.
articles.limitations: Cultural meanings may differ among participants and change over time. Some practices and records carry restrictions set by communities, and an archive needs their context and permissions.

articles.title: Oral traditions and performance
body: Communities can pass knowledge and expression through storytelling, song and performance. Words, melody, rhythm, movement and the relationships among participants can all matter. A story may take different forms when told at different times or by different people.

A recording can preserve one event. It can lose the ways people learn a performance, collaborate in it or decide when it is appropriate. In the UNESCO convention on living heritage, communities and practitioners have roles in identifying and safeguarding their practices. A record about one tradition needs its own context.
articles.limitations: The archive contains a photograph of one dance performance and a record of one musical instrument. These visual objects convey limited information about rhythm, sound and community meaning.

articles.title: Centauri Archive and interstellar messages
body: Pioneer spacecraft carried a plaque with engraved diagrams. Voyager spacecraft carried Golden Records containing images and sounds. Voyager's cover provides diagrams intended to help a finder play the record and make sense of its stored images.

Centauri Archive is an independent project investigating a small self-describing record of Earth, life and humanity. Its digital development collection and experiments inform a proposed physical carrier. A feasibility proposal identifies Fermi Explorer as a possible collaborator. No archive payload allocation, approval or integration agreement is confirmed.
articles.limitations: A framing method, archival package or proposal does not establish the physical artifact's survival, readout, interpretation, or mission acceptance.
